title: Palomar transients missing in Earth's shadow

tellings.quote:
said, "Yeah, you know, these objects

illuminated by the sun?"
And guess what? We get a huge deficit.
tellings.difference: Told first hand by Villarroel. She calls it a huge deficit, places it at geosynchronous distance and credits Guy Nir.
tellings.link_reason: Both tell of the Palomar transients being missing inside Earth's shadow.

as_told.title: Earth's shadow test shows a deficit of transients
as_told.place_text: Palomar plates; about 42,164 km from Earth (geosynchronous distance)

plain: Old sky photographs taken at Palomar Observatory in California between 1949 and 1957 show brief flashes of light that appear and then vanish. Few of them fall inside Earth's shadow, which is what you would expect if they were sunlit objects circling the planet. The astronomer Beatriz Villarroel describes the work on the show. She leads VASCO, a project comparing old sky surveys with modern ones. She explains that when her team checked a sample of these flashes against Earth's shadow, "guess what? We get a huge deficit." She places the objects at geosynchronous distance, the height where an orbit keeps pace with Earth's turning. She credits a colleague, Guy Nir, with the work. Michels sums up the finding in another episode: the objects disappear on the dark side of Earth, where the sun cannot light them. If the reading holds, something reflective was orbiting Earth in the early 1950s.
